body_html:
Imagine growing up as the most digitally connected generation in human history. For Generation Alpha -- roughly, those born since the early 2010s -- the smartphone arrived before the school bus did, and it has never really left.

"Generation Alpha has been completely formed by technology and screens and social media, meaning they've been on screens most of their life," Shane Pruitt, author of the book Reaching Generation Alpha: A Ministry Guide for Discipling the Church Beyond the Screen, told CBN News. The research backs him up: a majority of today's young people had regular access to tablets and smartphones before their teen years. Fourteen-year-old Kaileb Lewis said he got his first smartphone at age five. Tyiana Johnson, also fourteen, said she was seven or eight.

And the hours add up fast. Eleven-year-old Dallas Clark reported eight to twelve hours of screen time a day. Sixteen-year-old Lela Clayton said she spends five or six hours a day on her phone. Pruitt warns that this is about far more than entertainment. "I would even call it a discipleship war," he said. "Meaning if they have a screen, if they have a tablet, if they have a smartphone, they're being discipled by something or someone -- an algorithm, entertainer, a cultural agenda."

The cost is showing up in young hearts and minds. A recent Centers for Disease Control and Prevention study found that teenagers spending four or more hours a day on non-school screen time were more likely to report symptoms of anxiety and depression. Clayton sees it up close: "A lot of young people struggle with just a lot of mental issues and just being depressed. And it's really sad because sometimes there's no one there to really help them." Johnson was candid about where she turns: "I feel like my phone is my everything. I come to that when I feel depressed, down, anything."

So how can the church reach a generation raised on smartphones, social media, and artificial intelligence? According to the young people CBN News sat down with, the answer is not a slicker production. It is a relationship.

"I feel like building relationship is everything because you don't know what somebody else going through," said Johnson. Fifteen-year-old Sophie Knox, who became a Christian at age seven, put it this way: for young people to truly hear the gospel, they first have to trust the person sharing it. "You have to build a relationship with a student as you're preaching the gospel to them because you have to trust a person," she said.

Pruitt's point -- and the testimony of these teens -- is that the church's challenge is not really about technology at all. Every screen is competing to disciple this generation, and the church cannot out-algorithm the algorithm. What it can do is what it has always done: know young people by name, listen to them, and earn the trust that lets the gospel land. The medium has changed; the mission has not.

The next generation is not asking for a better app. They are asking whether anyone will get into their world -- and then tell them about the One who entered ours.

summary: Generation Alpha -- the most digitally connected generation in history -- is being discipled by algorithms and entertainers, says Shane Pruitt, author of "Reaching Generation Alpha." In interviews with CBN News, teens describe hours of daily screen time, rising anxiety, and one clear plea to the church: build a genuine relationship, and earn our trust.
takeaway: Paul said, "I am made all things to all men, that I might by all means save some" (1 Corinthians 9:22) -- not by lowering the gospel, but by entering people's world to reach them. The church cannot out-algorithm the algorithm, but it can do what no screen ever will: know a young soul by name and point it to Christ. "Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it" (Proverbs 22:6).
title: Beyond the Screen: 'Get Into Their World' -- How the Church Can Reach Generation Alpha for Jesus
